basic_info.name: fhir.resources (Python package, nazrulworld/fhir.resources)
basic_info.description: fhir.resources is a pure-Python library that provides Pydantic v2 model classes for every FHIR resource and data type, so a Python application can construct, parse, validate-by-type and serialise FHIR JSON, XML (experimental, via lxml) and YAML (experimental, via PyYAML) without a JVM. The single most load-bearing fact for MediKiosk Module C is its FHIR release matrix: from fhir.resources 7.0.0 onward there is NO FHIR R4 sub-package, the default models are R5 (5.0.0), and previous releases are shipped as sub-packages R4B (4.3.0) and STU3 (3.0.2) - the maintainer's stated position is that R4B is a near-compatible maintenance release that 'overlaps' R4, so it is recommended to move to R4B rather than keep R4. ABDM's NRCeS Implementation Guide is FHIR R4 (4.0.1), so Module C cannot rely on an R4 model package from current versions and must either use the R4B sub-package and accept any R4-vs-R4B drift, or pin the old 6.x line for genuine R4. The second load-bearing fact is that fhir.resources is a model/serialisation library, NOT a conformance validator: it enforces Pydantic type and cardinality checks but explicitly does NOT enforce enum/ValueSet constraints by default and performs no FHIRPath invariant or profile/IG validation, its own README says 'This feature is not available' for built-in custom validators and tells users to attach their own root validators. It is BSD-licensed, maintained essentially single-handedly by Md Nazrul Islam (nazrulworld), and is lightweight enough to run on a constrained offline kiosk - but it cannot certify NRCeS conformance on its own.
basic_info.organization: Maintained by Md Nazrul Islam (GitHub: nazrulworld), a single individual maintainer; occasional community pull requests (e.g. shaikn6, mschoettle, cybernop, ItayGoren). Originally generated from the forked nazrulworld/fhir-parser code generator. No company or foundation owns it. Note: README credits the FHIR trademark to HL7 International but the project is not an HL7 product.
basic_info.country: Maintainer based outside India (individual open-source developer, widely believed to be Bangladesh/South-Asia based; exact location not stated on the repository). The package itself is used internationally and is not India-specific. [uncertain]
basic_info.status: Production/stable, actively maintained but low-velocity and single-maintainer. PyPI classifier is 'Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable'. Current release 8.3.0 (2026-07-03); 8.3.1 is in development. The repository was pushed on 2026-09-14 and there are commits through June-September 2026, with 57 open issues and 127 forks. Not deprecated, not archived; bus-factor risk from the one-maintainer model is the main lifecycle caveat.

technical_features.what_it_does: fhir.resources exposes one Python class per FHIR resource and data type (e.g. Patient, Composition, Bundle, Organization, CodeableConcept, Extension) for FHIR R5, R4B and STU3, built on Pydantic v2. An application can instantiate classes directly, build them from JSON dicts/strings/files (model_validate / model_validate_json), serialise back to canonical FHIR JSON (model_dump / model_dump_json), and optionally to XML (model_dump_xml, model_validate_xml, with the ability to pass an lxml XMLSchema for validation against a FHIR .xsd) and YAML. Validation is the Pydantic layer: field types, list vs single cardinality, required-element presence, date/decimal/url/i d primitive formats, and FHIR primitive-extension handling (the '_fieldname' convention). It supports the FHIR 'summary' search mode in serialisation, FHIR comments (fhir_comments), and monkey-patchable constraints such as max id length and allowing empty strings. For Module C it is the natural way to build an OPConsultRecord/Bundle object graph in Python and emit canonical JSON, but it is not a conformance engine - it will not tell you whether the result satisfies the NRCeS ABDM profiles.
technical_features.architecture: Layered pure-Python package: fhir.resources.<resource> core classes for the default R5 release, with fhir.resources.R4B.* and fhir.resources.STU3.* sub-packages for older releases; shared primitive/datatype machinery (fhirtypes) and an abstract base (fhir.resources.fhirabstractmodel.FHIRAbstractModel, deriving from Pydantic BaseModel). Models are machine-generated by the forked nazrulworld/fhir-parser from the HL7 FHIR specification, so structure mirrors the spec exactly. Extension points: add_root_validator for custom cross-field rules, json_schema_extra metadata carrying enum_values and enum_reference_types, a custom JSON encoder, and the fhir-core companion package (>=1.1.9) that holds shared types, constraints and XML utilities. Installation extras: [yaml] adds PyYAML, [xml] adds lxml, [all] adds both. No server, no database, no network dependency at import time.
technical_features.inputs: JSON dicts, JSON strings/bytes, or files containing FHIR resources in JSON; experimental XML and YAML strings/files; native Python constructor arguments. It consumes already-structured FHIR data only - it does not ingest patient dialogue, audio, PDFs/scans, free text narratives or vitals semantics; any OCR/NLP/transcription must happen upstream and produce FHIR-shaped values before this library is involved.
technical_features.outputs: Typed Python objects and canonical FHIR JSON (or XML/YAML) for any FHIR resource, including a Composition-based OPConsultRecord document, a Bundle/transaction Bundle, Patient, Organization, Practitioner and Observation resources. It can also validate provided XML against an XML Schema and strip/emit FHIR comments. It does NOT produce a clinical summary, does not generate narrative text, and does not produce a validation verdict against a profile.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Tracks the HL7 FHIR specification structurally: default R5 (5.0.0), previous R4B (4.3.0) and STU3 (3.0.2) as sub-packages. Conformance is structural, not profile-level. Critically, there is NO FHIR R4 sub-package from version 7.0.0 onward - the maintainer's documented stance is that R4B 'comes with not that much changes over R4' and overlaps it, and users are advised to migrate to R4B; the last versions where R4 was the default line were 6.x (6.4.0 R4-default, 6.5.0 R4B-overlapped-R4). This is a direct mismatch with ABDM/NRCeS, which mandates FHIR R4 (4.0.1): the R4B model classes are the closest available modern substitute and are claimed to be largely compatible, but any R4-vs-R4B element differences (documented by HL7's R4B diff page) are not detected or flagged by this library. There is no support for loading StructureDefinitions, Implementation Guides, NRCeS ndhm.in profiles, ValueSet/terminology bindings or FHIRPath invariants, and enum constraints are explicitly NOT enforced automatically ('fhir.resources is providing API for enum constraint ... but it-self doesn't enforce enum based validation'). SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD and AYUSH/NAMASTE correctness are therefore wholly the caller's responsibility. A limited form of conformance checking is possible only for XML, by supplying a custom lxml schema parser (e.g. patient.xsd) at load time.
technical_features.offline_capability: Fully offline. It is a local pip-installable Python library with no network calls, no cloud service and no licence check; once installed it works air-gapped. This aligns well with MediKiosk's offline-first and India data-residency constraints, since all construction and serialisation happen in-process on the kiosk. There is no built-in encryption, local store or store-and-forward sync - anonymisation, at-rest encryption and sync are the kiosk application's responsibility.
technical_features.languages_supported: Not a natural-language tool: strings are carried verbatim, so Hindi/Devanagari/Hinglish text stored in CodeableConcept.text, Narrative or string fields round-trips as ordinary Unicode/Python str. No tokenisation, transliteration, translation or bilingual rendering, and no special handling of Devanagari beyond standard Python 3 UTF-8 behaviour. [uncertain] AYUSH/NAMASTE terminology awareness is absent.
technical_features.deployment_model: On-device or embedded Python runtime - pip install fhir.resources (optionally [all] for XML/YAML). Requires Python >=3.8 (classifiers list 3.8 through 3.14) and Pydantic v2 (pulled in transitively along with fhir-core). Pure Python, no GPU, no JVM, very small footprint relative to Java/.NET FHIR stacks, which makes it well suited to an offline ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk as the in-kiosk serialisation layer. It is not a server and should not be treated as one; if a queryable FHIR store or IG validator is needed, that belongs on a clinic/HIS-side service (e.g. HAPI or the HL7 validator CLI).

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Not an ML/statistical system, so there are no accuracy, F1, ROUGE or BERTScore figures. Its quality signal is test coverage and round-trip fidelity: the project publishes a Codecov badge and runs tox-based test suites across supported Python versions, and its design goal is that serialised output matches the FHIR specification key order. The maintainer's 8.2.0/8.3.0 notes mention tighter typing and a test suite that also exercises communication with a HAPI server. No numeric coverage percentage or conformance-pass-rate is published. [uncertain]
performance_metrics.latency: No official latency or throughput benchmarks are published. The README's only performance claim is qualitative - Pydantic v2 makes the package 'faster in performance'. For Module C, constructing and serialising a single OPConsultRecord Bundle is a CPU-bound, in-process operation expected to be negligible next to OCR/ASR/NLU, but no measured figure exists. [uncertain]
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Pure Python; requirements are Python >=3.8, Pydantic v2, and fhir-core>=1.1.9, with optional PyYAML/lxml. No GPU or significant VRAM; footprint is small (models plus a handful of dependencies), which fits the ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk comfortably. It is one of the lightest ways to handle FHIR in an offline kiosk. No published RAM/CPU minimums, but they are effectively those of the Python interpreter plus Pydantic. [uncertain]
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: At verification: 535 GitHub stars, 127 forks, 15 watchers, 467 commits, 57 open issues, 127 forks. PyPI install counts are surfaced through a pepy.tech badge but no precise download number was captured. It is one of the two or three most used FHIR model libraries in Python (alongside fhirclient for network work and fhirpathpy for queries) - clearly the default for typed FHIR in Python. [uncertain] exact download volume.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: There is no clinical or human evaluation and none is appropriate. Quality is established through automated test suites (tox, pytest), Codecov-tracked coverage, and round-trip serialisation tests, plus continuing compatibility fixes tied to GitHub issues (e.g. Pydantic 2.11 deprecation handling, pyright/mypy typing fixes, mypy py.typed marker). For Module C the meaningful evaluation is to build a known OPConsultRecord bundle with the R4B models and confirm it round-trips and that its shape matches the NRCeS IG - which this library cannot itself certify, so an external validator is required.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Module C must construct and emit a structured, physician-ready summary as an NRCeS-profile OPConsultRecord (a Composition within a FHIR R4 DocumentBundle). fhir.resources is the most ergonomic Python route to build that object graph, enforce basic type/cardinality correctness at construction time, and emit canonical FHIR JSON offline on the kiosk - especially valuable given MediKiosk's Python-friendly AI/OCR/ASR stack and CPU-only, no-JVM kiosk. It is also a useful guardrail: Pydantic will reject malformed types and missing mandatory base-spec elements before anything reaches ABDM. The critical caveat it surfaces for the design is version mismatch - ABDM is FHIR R4 while current fhir.resources ships R4B (not R4), so Module C must consciously decide between the R4B sub-package with a documented compatibility rationale or pinning the older 6.x R4 line, and must not assume this library's 'validation' equals NRCeS profile conformance. It supplies the construction/serialisation tier, not the conformance-assurance tier nor any elicitation, summarisation or digitisation.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) fhir.resources as the in-Python model/serialisation layer for building the OPConsultRecord Bundle, because it is lightweight, offline and idiomatic for a Python pipeline; (2) its Pydantic type/cardinality validation as a cheap first gate that catches malformed values before a heavier validator runs; (3) its add_root_validator mechanism to encode Module C-specific business rules (e.g. mandatory provenance/attestation fields, AYUSH coding presence) as explicit, testable cross-field checks; (4) its XML-schema hook (lxml) only if a hard XML profile is ever needed, since production ABDM exchange is JSON. Reject or adapt: (1) do NOT treat fhir.resources as the conformance gate - its own docs state enum constraints are not enforced and custom/profile validation is 'not available', so pair it with HAPI's validator or the HL7 validator_cli against the NRCeS ndhm.in package; (2) do NOT default to R5 models - explicitly import the R4B sub-package (or pin 6.x for true R4) and record why, because R5 output is not ABDM-valid and R4B is only claimed to overlap R4; (3) reject relying on YAML/XML experimental serialisation for ABDM payloads (JSON is the validated path and XML/YAML are flagged as experimental); (4) accept that single-maintainer governance means Module C should pin a tested version rather than track latest, and be prepared to maintain local forks/patches if the maintainer goes dormant.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: The dominant risks are: (a) no FHIR R4 sub-package from v7, while ABDM mandates R4 - R4B is a substitute by policy, not a guarantee, and HL7 documents real R4-to-R4B differences, so silent divergence is possible; (b) it is not a conformance validator - enum/ValueSet constraints are not enforced, FHIRPath invariants and profile/IG rules are not evaluated at all, and reference-type constraints are only exposed as metadata, meaning a structurally 'valid' Pydantic object can still be rejected by ABDM; (c) single-maintainer bus-factor: essentially one person (nazrulworld) owns the generator, the fork, and the releases, and despite commits in 2026 the cadence is low (8.1.0 in Jul 2025, 8.2.0 in Feb 2026, 8.3.0 in Jul 2026), with 57 open issues; (d) generation-based models can lag specification errata and community fixes; (e) breaking changes do occur across majors (v7 relocated R4B under a sub-package and changed cache keys; v8 requires Pydantic v2; v8.3.0 made Extension.url required) and can surprise an unpinned consumer; (f) the licence text is a BSD-3-Clause-style document but GitHub's licensee reports NOASSERTION/Other, so an automated licence scanner at a government procurement gate could flag it and need manual review; (g) no AYUSH/NAMASTE, bilingual or terminology support whatsoever.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: fhir.resources is a build-time/on-device construction library, not a competitor, and it neither strengthens nor erodes MediKiosk's differentiation on its own - it is agnostic to offline, India-residency, NRCeS, provenance and attestation. It helps MediKiosk execute the 'NRCeS-conformant emission' claim cheaply in Python but provides zero conformance assurance, so that differentiator still rests on Module C's validator pipeline and its documented R4/R4B decision. Its real strategic value is negative-but-useful: it is concrete evidence that the Python FHIR ecosystem has a live FHIR-version gap for R4 versus ABDM, which MediKiosk can turn into a stated, tests-backed design decision (R4B-with-rationale or pinned-R4) that many ABDM entrants gloss over. It does nothing on elicitation, AYUSH clinical content, bilingual summaries or physician attestation, so it cannot substitute for Module C's differentiators.

business_info.license: BSD 3-Clause-style licence. PyPI metadata and the setup.py/Trove classifier say 'BSD license', and the repository LICENSE file contains the standard three-clause BSD text ('BSD License', 'Copyright (c) 2019, Md Nazrul Islam'), including the non-endorsement clause. However, GitHub's automated licensee detects it as NOASSERTION/Other rather than SPDX 'BSD-3-Clause', so the exact SPDX identifier may need manual confirmation in a formal/open-source-scan review. Permissive: commercial and closed-source use allowed with attribution; no copyleft.
business_info.pricing: Free and open source (pip install fhir.resources). No paid tier, no commercial support offering.
business_info.funding: Unfunded volunteer/individual project. No venture, foundation grant or corporate backing was found; the PEPY downloads badge and GitHub Sponsors-style presence are the only visible support channels. [uncertain] Whether opencollective/GitHub Sponsors funding is active was not confirmed.
business_info.commercial_status: Free community open-source project (unpaid), maintained by an individual rather than a company or government programme.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Other ways to handle FHIR in Python: pydantic-fhir / fhir.resources-style generators; the Firely .NET SDK and HAPI FHIR (Java) if a JVM is acceptable; the HL7 org.hl7.fhir.core validator and HAPI for validation; fhirclient (Python) for FHIR REST; pymongo-style generic JSON handling; and language-agnostic options like the FHIR Shorthand (FSH)/SUSHI toolchain, HL7's validator_cli, and matchbox for profile validation. For the specific R4 gap, the practical alternatives to fhir.resources are (i) the older 6.x fhir.resources line for true R4 models, or (ii) building/validating on the JVM with HAPI/validator_cli against the NRCeS package. Nothing in Python directly competes on 'typed R4 model classes maintained as an IG validator' - fhir.resources explicitly does not do IG validation.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: Interoperates with the Python data/AI ecosystem: Pydantic v2 models plug into FastAPI (request/response models), ORMs, JSON/YAML loaders and the fhir-core companion package for types and XML utilities. It does not itself integrate with HIS/EHR vendors, HAPI FHIR, the ABDM gateway (HIP/HIU/PHR roles), health lockers or messaging; any such integration is done in the host application. There is no native connection to the NRCeS ndhm.in package or terminologies. In practice it is commonly paired with fhirclient or requests for transport and with HAPI/validator_cli for conformance.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The Python FHIR ecosystem is fragmented and lower-budget than the JVM/.NET side, and fhir.resources being effectively single-maintainer is representative of that. The concrete ecosystem signal for MediKiosk is the R4-versus-R4B drift: because the generator followed HL7's recommendation to treat R4B as the R4 successor, Python tooling is nudged away from the exact FHIR R4 that ABDM/NRCeS still mandates, whereas HAPI and the HL7 validator remain R4-first-class. This means choosing a Python-only FHIR path introduces a small but real version-management obligation for ABDM work, and the safest posture is Python for modelling plus a JVM/CLI validator for the NRCeS conformance gate. No Indian government programme, NRCeS, or ABDM-specific tooling is built on or endorses this library.

history.release_date: First PyPI release lineage starts around 2019; the repository was created on GitHub on 2019-01-11, with 4.0.0b1/4.0.0 in January 2019 as early releases, 5.0.0 (2019-06-08) as the first stable, and 6.0.0b1 (2020-07-05) as the 'fully rewritten' release.
history.key_milestones: 2019-01-11 repository created; 2019 4.x/5.x early model releases and DSTU2 support. 2020-07-05 6.0.0b1 full rewrite on modern Python; 2020-12-17 6.0.0. 2022-05-11 6.4.0 (R4 default); 2023-01-01 6.5.0 overlaps R4B over R4. 2023-04-08 7.0.0 - R5 becomes default, R4B moved under the R4B sub-package, no R4 sub-package thereafter. 2023-12-14 7.1.0 - drops Pydantic v1, moves to Pydantic v2 APIs. 2024-12-25 8.0.0 - fhir-core 1.0.0, XML serialisation, DSTU2 removed, Python 3.7 dropped. 2025-07-10 8.1.0 - FHIR 'summary' mode, typing/CI fixes. 2026-02-02 8.2.0 - type aliases, fhir-core 1.1.5. 2026-07-03 8.3.0 - Extension.url now required, fhir-core floor 1.1.9.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Within the Mar-Sep 2026 window the project shipped 8.3.0 on 2026-07-03 (making the FHIR Extension.url field mandatory - a breaking change - and raising the minimum fhir-core dependency to 1.1.9), and the repository shows continuing maintenance: commits through late June 2026 adding error logging for HAPI-server responses and tests for 412 status handling, a docs pull request merged on 2026-09-14, and 8.3.1 left in development. GitHub reports pushed_at 2026-09-14. So while the maintainer remains active in the window, there was no substantial feature release beyond 8.3.0, and there is still no sign of an FHIR R4 sub-package being reintroduced. Nothing in the window changes the R4/R4B mismatch for ABDM.

market_positioning.target_users: Python developers and data/AI engineers building healthcare applications, FHIR APIs (often with FastAPI), research pipelines, or FHIR data-processing that needs typed FHIR objects; health-IT integrators who prefer Python over Java/.NET. It is a developer library, not an end-user product, and it is not aimed at clinicians, patients or hospitals directly.
market_positioning.market_segment: FHIR tooling / healthcare interoperability model libraries for the Python stack - the object-model and serialisation layer, adjacent to (but not overlapping) FHIR servers, IG validators and terminology services. It is not an intake, ambient-scribing, PHR, AYUSH-software, diagnostics-kiosk or benchmarking product.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: It positions itself as 'FHIR Resources as Model Class' and 'FHIR Resources (R5, R4B, STU3)' - a Pydantic-v2-powered Python library that 'provides tools and classes for all of the FHIR Resources defined in the FHIR specification, and allows you to create and manipulate FHIR resources in Python', emphasising easy construction, extensible validation, easy export, ORM compatibility, full primitive-extension support, availability of previous FHIR releases as sub-packages, and a BSD licence. Its own README is candid about the R4/R4B trade-off and about not enforcing enum constraints.
